item.title: Why You Can Be Proud of Yourself After Psychosis
item.description:
Psychosis

Why You Can Be Proud of Yourself After Psychosis

Personal Perspective: You are a survivor and own your recovery.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Perception is not always reality — especially with overwhelming negative emotions.
  • You can't depend on others to accept you and be proud of you, you must cultivate it within.
  • Stigma places more importance on other people's reactions to you than how you see yourself.
  • Persistence during recovery, refusing to quit, means you can take pride in owning your recovery.
Conflicting Emotions about Self-Acceptance and Pride
Source: AdobeStock / Ryker

In my way of defining emotional recovery, I emphasize three components: trusting yourself, believing in yourself, and wanting to be you. Of course, these three components can be broken down into many more components. In the final phase of emotional recovery, wanting to be you again, I think that you must first establish pride in who you are, before, during, and after your acute illness. I know for me, pride was the last emotion I could comprehend regaining after my psychotic breaks, but it was pride that was critical to developing my current state of well-being and the progress I have made over the years.

I lost my sense of pride when I lost my mind and was cognitively impaired after having been an academic, a path that came to a halt. My sense of pride was lost after navigating a psych ward and losing my sense of autonomy. I lost my pride when I felt embarrassed and ashamed for how I acted during my breaks in front of my family and friends. I felt terrible that communicating my hallucinations scared others. I was so ashamed that for years other people knew something was off about me, but I didn’t always realize it, and when I was aware, there was nothing I could do about it.

Being Proud of Being Alive

I think it’s easy to take for granted that you are alive after being stabilized on medicine after a break. Since you often live in an alternate reality during a break, you can make choices that can cost you your life. I did several things due to my breaks that could have cost me my life. The scariest thing is that no one can reason with you, and you cannot even reason with yourself. You can’t second guess yourself, and everything is as real as the fact that I am typing now.

And you are not just lucky to be alive—you probably made some essential decisions that led to you being alive today. Maybe you agreed to hospitalization, maybe you consented to medicine, or maybe you did not consent to anything. But it doesn’t matter as much as the fact that you are alive and breathing right now. You do have a future, whether you believe it or not.

It took me awhile to want to be alive again, so I did not feel proud of being alive at first. It took me a long time to sense that being alive is a blessing and an accomplishment and not something to take for granted. I emphasize this because I hope it takes you less time to feel this way than it did for me.

Being Proud of Being You as an Individual

I was utterly humiliated and ashamed of being me. I seriously thought of moving to a new city and starting over where no one I met could possibly know that I used to be mentally ill. The worst was not knowing who knew what had happened, or knowing there were people who silently knew I was becoming ill before my breaks happened, even when I didn’t. I’m glad I didn’t move, though. To make the decision to stay put meant I was facing inner fears and insecurities head on instead of fleeing from them. Geography rarely gives you an escape from inner problems.

The biggest battle to win is caring more about how you feel about yourself than what others think of you. So much of the stigma in this illness is detrimental because it tells you to put yourself last, and put what anybody else in the world could possibly think of you as more important. We look to others as a mirror for how we see ourselves. Their approval means we can approve of ourselves, but that is a risky and dangerous way to find identity and self-acceptance. I’ve done that myself, but in doing so, I gave everyone else power over my life and my feelings.

You can’t wait for someone else to be proud of you, especially when you are an adult. Even when I was devasted over my schizophrenia diagnosis and embarrassed, my life was mine, and my parents were not shaken like I was—they still accepted me without judgment. While that was so important to me, at some point, I had to adopt that stance myself and not depend on other people to supply it.

You Can Still Have a Life You Are Proud Of

No matter how bleak and meaningless your life seems, you have to remember this is your perspective on reality—it is not necessarily reality itself. In my teens I was a very negative thinker as part of my depression, and I saw my perception as the only way to look at things. However, it was huge when I could understand that my interpretations were just one vantage point, and other people’s interpretations may be just as valid, or even more accurate.

I saw my life as condemned and unfixable. I didn’t even think a sovereign God could fix my life. I would open my eyes every morning, but did not have enough motivation to get out of bed or have any direction forward, either in a momentary sense or long-term. However, I am so thankful that, even though I was hurting so bad inside and had no idea what point there could be to my life, that I continued to wake up each morning and eventually get out of bed. Sometimes there was little daily structure in early recovery, but maybe I would wash the dishes for my mother, maybe I would walk my dog, maybe I would try to concentrate and read something, or maybe I would look presentable for company coming over. In other words, I could take little daily actions that gave me a sense of accomplishment and pride.

What 14 Years in Remission Has Turned Into for Me

In the 14 years after my last break, I’ve assigned meaning to these times through helping others, and I’ve never been more proud of myself, in the sense that I want to be me. I embrace my identity now, and I’m proud in the sense that I totally own my recovery. I’m proud that I did not quit, and I kept going to psychiatry appointments and therapy appointments. Even when I wasn’t sure if they were making a difference, I did so out of the principle of self-care and trying. Over time, all my appointments I kept have made a huge difference. By finally caring more about myself than what the world thinks of my illness, I pulled myself out of the mire and rebuilt my identity based on what I feel is a fully authentic existence.

I’m a survivor, and you are too. The goals are positive self-talk, regaining your sense of pride in owning your recovery, being yourself and no one else, and authentically reshaping your future in a way that makes you even better than you were before.

item.title: 5 Reasons Exceptional Leaders Invest in Mental Health
item.description:
Leadership

5 Reasons Exceptional Leaders Invest in Mental Health

Why healthy minds yield the greatest dividends.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Fifty-three percent of employees report feeling burned out.
  • Exceptional leaders recognize that employees need to be well, before they can perform well.
  • Great leaders see mental health as a strategic asset.

Strategic thinking is underrated.

I took an economics class when I was a freshman in college. On the first day of class my professor said, “You'll do well in this course if you think strategically and understand that every action has a consequence, every choice has a cost, and everything is connected.” That lesson has stayed with me over the years — not just in economics, but in leadership.

The best leaders think the same way.

They understand that employee mental health is not an isolated issue tucked away in Human Resources. It is connected to decision-making, innovation, engagement, retention, customer service, organizational culture, and ultimately, the financial health of the company.

Exceptional leaders recognize that employees need to be well, before they can perform well.

Leading people means understanding that the quality of an employee's mental health directly influences the quality of his or her performance. Healthy minds solve problems more effectively, communicate more clearly, recover from setbacks more quickly, and make better decisions under pressure.

Conversely, chronic stress quietly degrades concentration, judgment, creativity, and motivation, which can lead to absenteeism.

The financial implications are staggering.

According to the Deloitte Center for Health Solutions, mental health inequities cost U.S. businesses approximately $115 billion annually through absenteeism and workforce attrition. Those numbers represent lost dollars and even more lost potential.

Throughout my career as a psychotherapist, workplace mental health educator, and leadership trainer, I have been privileged to work with some of the world's most respected organizational leaders. Although they represent different industries and leadership styles, the most exceptional among them share one defining characteristic.

They see employee mental health as a strategic asset.

One executive leading a large pharmaceutical division explained, "As a condition of hiring, I require every employee to submit a personal self-care plan. Mental health isn't a buzzword here. Caring for yourself is part of our culture."

He went on to explain that every employee schedules vacation time well in advance. He shared, "Walking in balance is part of our mission. It's part of employee performance."

That leader understood something neuroscience has repeatedly confirmed; human beings are not designed for continuous output. The brain performs best when periods of focused effort are balanced by adequate recovery.

I explain to my audiences, We can’t run our lives like we handle our cellphones. We must take time to unplug, or we hit walls.

Organizations ignore this reality at their own expense.

According to the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI), fifty-three percent of employees report feeling burned out because of their jobs, while thirty-five percent say their mental health has negatively affected their performance at work.

Behind every statistic is a person. During one employee wellness focus group, a woman quietly admitted, "My body is sitting at my desk, but my mind is consumed with raising three children by myself and feeling completely isolated." She estimated she was functioning at only five to ten percent of her potential.

What made her disclosure especially sobering was the nature of her work. She performed detailed calculations involving toxic chemical compounds. The truth is, she had herself and her organization at risk, daily!

Her story represents a growing population I describe as functionally, chronically stressed employees; individuals who continue showing up every day while quietly operating far below their cognitive and emotional capacity.

From the outside, they appear productive. Inside, they are depleted.

No organization can eliminate stress entirely, nor should it attempt to. Stress is part of meaningful work and meaningful lives.

However, exceptional leaders understand they have both an opportunity and a responsibility to create cultures where employees have access to education, resources, and practical tools that strengthen psychological resilience before stress becomes burnout.

The question is no longer whether leaders should invest in employee mental health. The real question is whether organizations can afford not to.

Here are five reasons exceptional leaders recognize mental health as a strategic asset.

Mental health improves decision-making

The human brain was never designed to make complex decisions under prolonged emotional distress. When stress becomes chronic, the brain naturally shifts its resources toward survival. Attention narrows, and risk assessment becomes distorted. Employees become more reactive than reflective.

A former client, who was a construction worker, shared, “My co-worker always comes to work half asleep. Today I think I prevented a serious accident. He did not secure the load to the crane properly, and I caught his mistake just in time!”

My client was taking care of himself, mind, body, and soul. I am convinced that he also helped the company avoid a potential lawsuit that day. The damage would have been catastrophic if he were not on his toes.

Mental health increases engagement and team cohesion

People perform their best when they feel psychologically safe. Employees who believe they can ask questions, admit mistakes, contribute ideas, and seek support without fear are more likely to collaborate, innovate, and remain engaged. Trust fuels teamwork.

Psychological safety fuels trust. Exceptional leaders intentionally build environments where both can flourish. When employees feel that their employer is "looking out for their best interest," it builds a lasting sense of goodwill.

Mental health reduces costly burnout and turnover

Burnout doesn't usually arrive wearing a name tag.

It sneaks in disguised as "I'll just work through lunch."

Then it becomes, "I'll answer emails tonight."

Then, "I'll take vacation next year."

Before long, exhaustion has become the company culture.

Exceptional leaders interrupt that cycle before employees convince themselves that chronic stress is simply "part of the job."

Mental health fuels creativity, collaboration, innovation, and loyalty

Creativity requires mental space. Anxiety and depression make people feel boxed in. Employees consumed by worry rarely have extra cognitive bandwidth to develop breakthrough ideas. Healthy employees do. They ask better questions, take thoughtful risks, and, because they feel cared for, they become far more invested in helping the organization succeed. People rarely forget how a workplace made them feel.

Mental health builds resilient, high-performing organizational cultures

Culture isn't what appears on the company's website. It's what employees joke about in the parking lot after work.

If everyone laughs about never taking vacation...that's culture.

If everyone quietly competes over who sleeps the least...that's culture.

If employees proudly tell new hires, “Take care of yourself here. Leadership actually means it,"… that's culture too.

Exceptional leaders know that resilience isn't asking people to carry heavier loads forever.

It's giving them the tools to recover, recharge, and continue carrying the mission forward.

The organizations that thrive in the decades ahead will not simply have the smartest strategies. They will have leaders wise enough to recognize that their greatest strategic advantage has never been technology, buildings, or balance sheets.

It has always been the health of the human minds entrusted to carry the mission forward.
